notes: Original lectures (batch 3 of 3). Each lecture feeds eight types: RL, SST, LMCMA, LFIB, HCS, LMCSA, SMW and HIW. Lectures 11 to 15 are backup questions.

sources.title: How herd immunity works
sources.body: When a large enough share of a population is immune to an infectious disease, the disease struggles to spread, even to people who are not immune. This is called herd immunity. It works because each infected person meets fewer people who can catch the disease, so chains of transmission break down. The share of people who need to be immune depends on how contagious the disease is. For measles, which spreads extremely easily, around ninety five percent of people need to be immune. For less contagious diseases, the threshold is lower. Herd immunity is especially important for people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies and patients with weakened immune systems. However, if vaccination rates fall even slightly below the threshold in a community, outbreaks can return quickly. The speaker stresses that high coverage must be maintained everywhere, not just on average.

sources.title: How eucalyptus forests recover from fire
sources.body: Many Australian eucalyptus forests have evolved alongside fire, and several species have remarkable ways of recovering. Some eucalypts have buds hidden deep beneath their thick bark. After a fire burns the leaves, these buds sprout, and within months the blackened trunks are covered in fresh green shoots. Other species have woody swellings at the base of the trunk, called lignotubers, which store energy and can produce new stems even if everything above ground is destroyed. A few species, such as mountain ash, are killed by intense fire but release huge numbers of seeds that grow quickly in the ash-rich soil. However, these strategies have limits. If fires return too frequently, young trees may burn before they are old enough to produce seeds. The speaker warns that more frequent fires could therefore change which species dominate these forests.

sources.title: Why central banks raise interest rates
sources.body: Central banks, such as the Reserve Bank of Australia, are usually responsible for keeping inflation low and stable. Their main tool is the official interest rate, which influences the rates that commercial banks charge on loans and pay on savings. When inflation is too high, a central bank may raise interest rates. Borrowing becomes more expensive, so households with mortgages have less money to spend, and businesses may delay investment. Saving also becomes more attractive. As overall spending slows, firms find it harder to raise prices, and inflation gradually falls. The process takes time, often a year or more, which is why central banks try to forecast future conditions. Raising rates carries risks. If rates rise too far, unemployment can increase and the economy may enter a recession. The speaker describes monetary policy as a constant balancing act.

sources.title: The debate over deep sea mining
sources.body: On parts of the deep ocean floor lie potato-sized rocks called nodules, which contain valuable metals such as nickel, cobalt and manganese. These metals are used in batteries for electric vehicles and renewable energy storage, so some companies argue that mining the seabed could support the transition away from fossil fuels. Supporters also point out that land mining causes deforestation and affects local communities. However, many scientists urge caution. The deep sea is one of the least explored environments on Earth, and new species are discovered on almost every expedition. Nodules grow extremely slowly, over millions of years, and many animals live on or around them. Mining machines would also create clouds of sediment that could spread over wide areas. Several countries have called for a pause until the environmental effects are better understood. The speaker supports this cautious approach.

sources.title: Music and the brain
sources.body: Listening to music activates many parts of the brain at once, including areas involved in hearing, movement, memory and emotion. When we hear a piece of music we enjoy, the brain releases dopamine, a chemical linked to pleasure and reward. Interestingly, dopamine is released not only at the most exciting moment, but also in the seconds before it, as we anticipate what is coming. Learning to play an instrument appears to strengthen connections between brain regions, and some studies find that musicians are better at detecting small differences in sound, which may help with learning languages. Claims that simply listening to classical music makes children more intelligent, however, have not been supported by careful research. Music is also used in therapy, for example to help stroke patients recover speech. The speaker concludes that active participation matters more than passive listening.

sources.title: Harnessing tidal energy
sources.body: Tides are driven by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun, so, unlike wind and sunshine, they can be predicted years in advance. This makes tidal energy attractive to electricity grid operators, who need to match supply with demand. There are two main approaches. Tidal barrages are dams built across estuaries; water flows through turbines as the tide rises and falls. They can generate large amounts of power, but they are very expensive and can change the habitats of birds and fish. Tidal stream turbines work more like underwater wind turbines, placed in channels where currents are strong. They have less impact on the landscape, but saltwater, strong currents and marine growth make maintenance difficult. Only a few suitable sites exist worldwide. The speaker suggests that tidal energy will remain a small but valuable part of the energy mix.

sources.title: The Roman road network
sources.body: At its height, the Roman Empire was connected by more than eighty thousand kilometres of paved roads. These roads were built mainly for military purposes, allowing soldiers to move quickly to troubled regions. Roman engineers preferred straight routes where possible, and they built roads in layers: large stones at the bottom, then gravel and sand, and finally tightly fitted paving stones on top. The surface was slightly curved so that rainwater would drain into ditches on each side. Although built for armies, the roads also transformed trade and communication. Merchants, officials and messengers used them, and towns grew up along major routes. A system of official stations allowed messengers to change horses and travel long distances in a single day. Many modern roads in Europe still follow Roman routes, which the speaker sees as evidence of remarkably careful planning.

sources.title: Where food waste happens
sources.body: Roughly a third of the food produced in the world is lost or wasted. Where this happens depends on the country. In lower income countries, most losses occur early in the supply chain, because of poor storage, a lack of refrigeration and difficulties transporting crops to market. In wealthier countries, a larger share is wasted by shops and households. Supermarkets may reject fruit and vegetables that look imperfect, and consumers often buy more than they need or throw food away because they misunderstand date labels. Food waste matters for the environment because producing food uses land, water and energy, and rotting food in landfill releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Solutions therefore differ. Better storage helps farmers in some regions, while clearer labels and smaller portions help elsewhere. The speaker argues that solutions must match the local causes.

sources.title: Citizen science and bird counts
sources.body: Citizen science means involving members of the public in collecting scientific data. Bird surveys are one of the most successful examples. In New Zealand, for instance, thousands of households take part in an annual garden bird survey, spending one hour counting the birds they see in their gardens or local parks. No single count is very precise, but when thousands of observations are combined over many years, clear trends emerge, such as which species are becoming more common in towns. Professional scientists could never collect data on this scale by themselves. Citizen science also raises public awareness and interest in conservation. There are challenges, however. Volunteers vary in skill, and more people take part in some areas than others. Researchers deal with this by providing identification guides and using statistical methods that account for uneven effort. The speaker describes volunteers as partners in research.

sources.title: Storing carbon in farm soils
sources.body: Soils contain more carbon than the atmosphere and all living plants combined. Much of it comes from roots, fallen leaves and other organic matter that has been broken down by microbes. Over centuries of ploughing and intensive farming, many agricultural soils have lost a large share of their original carbon. This has led to interest in practices that could put some of it back, such as planting cover crops between harvests, reducing ploughing, and managing grazing more carefully. Such practices can also improve soil structure and help soils hold water. However, measuring changes in soil carbon is difficult, because levels vary greatly across a single field and change slowly. Carbon stored in soil can also be released again if practices change or temperatures rise. The speaker concludes that soil carbon is worth pursuing, but it should not be treated as a substitute for reducing emissions.

sources.title: Artificial intelligence in medical imaging
sources.body: Medical imaging, such as X-rays and scans, produces enormous numbers of images that must be examined by specialists. Artificial intelligence systems trained on large collections of labelled images can now detect certain conditions, such as some lung diseases or signs of eye damage caused by diabetes, with accuracy similar to experienced doctors. These systems could reduce waiting times and help regions with too few specialists. However, several problems remain. A system trained on images from one hospital may perform worse in another, where different equipment is used or patients are from different populations. It can also be hard to understand why a system reached a particular decision. For these reasons, most experts see artificial intelligence as a tool that supports specialists rather than replaces them. The speaker adds that systems must be tested in real clinical settings, not just in laboratories.

sources.title: The remarkable flight of the bar-tailed godwit
sources.body: Every year, bar-tailed godwits make one of the longest non-stop journeys of any animal. After breeding in Alaska, they fly across the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand and eastern Australia, a flight of more than eleven thousand kilometres that can take around nine days. During this time, they do not stop to eat, drink or rest. To prepare, the birds feed intensively and roughly double their body weight, mostly by storing fat. Remarkably, their digestive organs shrink before departure, reducing unnecessary weight. Scientists have tracked individual birds with small satellite tags, revealing that they choose departure times when winds are favourable. On the return journey, godwits stop in East Asia to refuel on coastal mudflats. Many of these mudflats have been lost to development, which the speaker identifies as one of the greatest threats to the species.

sources.title: What happens when the minimum wage rises?
sources.body: A simple economic model predicts that raising the minimum wage will reduce employment, because businesses will hire fewer workers when labour becomes more expensive. For many years this was widely accepted. However, a number of studies comparing similar regions, where only one had increased its minimum wage, found little or no loss of jobs. Several explanations have been offered. Higher wages may reduce staff turnover, saving employers the cost of recruiting and training. Better paid workers may also be more productive, and some businesses may raise prices slightly or accept lower profits. Most economists now agree that moderate increases have small effects on employment. There is less agreement about very large increases, especially in regions where average wages are low. The speaker suggests that the size of the increase, relative to local wages, is what matters most.

sources.title: The effects of light pollution
sources.body: Artificial light at night has transformed human life, but it also has costs. Light pollution is the excessive or poorly directed use of outdoor lighting. It hides the stars from most city dwellers; many people have never seen the Milky Way. It also affects wildlife. Newly hatched sea turtles, for example, find the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, and bright coastal lights can lead them away from the sea. Many insects are drawn to lamps and die from exhaustion, and migrating birds can become disoriented. In humans, exposure to light at night can interfere with sleep hormones. Fortunately, light pollution is one of the easiest environmental problems to reduce. Shielding lights so that they point downwards, using warmer colours and switching lights off when not needed can all help. The speaker notes that these changes also save money.

sources.title: Tourism and carrying capacity
sources.body: Tourism brings jobs and income, but popular destinations can suffer when visitor numbers grow faster than local infrastructure. The idea of carrying capacity asks how many visitors a place can receive before the environment, services or quality of life for residents begin to decline. In Queenstown, for example, rapid growth in visitors has put pressure on housing, roads and water supply, while some famous walking tracks become crowded during peak season. Destinations respond in different ways. Some introduce booking systems or daily limits for sensitive sites, while others charge visitor levies to fund infrastructure. Encouraging travel outside peak months can also spread the pressure. Critics warn that high fees may make travel affordable only for wealthier visitors. The speaker argues that carrying capacity is not a fixed number, because good planning can raise it.
